overview.text: Feminism is both a body of ideas and a social movement seeking justice for women and an end to sexism. It challenges not only unequal laws or formal rights, but also social arrangements, cultural assumptions, and institutions that can restrict people’s opportunities. Feminist inquiry examines political, economic, social, and personal life, including work and family. Feminism is not one doctrine or a single agreed plan: activists and thinkers differ about what equality requires and how injustice works. Many also emphasize that gender-based injustice can overlap with racism, class inequality, and other forms of discrimination, so women’s experiences and priorities are not identical.

key_facts.text: Feminism is both a political movement and an intellectual commitment; its shared concern is justice for women and opposition to sexism, though its approaches and proposed remedies differ.
Feminist analysis can examine institutions and experiences often treated as private or ordinary, such as family life, care, work, sexuality, and the body.
The 1848 Seneca Falls women’s rights convention is commonly linked to the beginning of the organized U.S. movement; it called for rights including education, property, and political participation.
The history of women’s activism is broader than a simple sequence of “waves”; the wave metaphor can help describe eras, but their boundaries are not precise.
Intersectional approaches draw attention to how gender discrimination can combine with discrimination related to race, class, ethnicity, religion, or sexual orientation.
